children.html: Body appreciation, media influence, and weight status predict consideration of cosmetic surgery among female undergraduates
• aDepartment of Psychology, University of Westminster, UK
• bDepartment of Psychology, HELP University College, Malaysia
Article history: Received 30 April 2009 Received in revised form 3 July 2009 Accepted 4 July 2009
Keywords: Cosmetic surgery Media influence Body appreciation Body mass index

The current study examined the association between consideration of cosmetic surgery, body appreciation, media influence, and participant demographics. In total, 322 female university students completed the Consider subscale of the Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale, the third revision of Sociocultural Attitudes Toward Appearance Scale (SATAQ-3), the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), and provided their demographic details. Bivariate correlations showed that consideration of cosmetic surgery was significantly and positively correlated with three of the SATAQ-3 subscales and negatively correlated with BAS scores, age, and body mass index (BMI). A multiple regression showed that the only significant predictors of consideration of cosmetic surgery were greater media influence, less body appreciation, and lower BMI. These results are discussed in relation to the extant literature on attitudes towards cosmetic surgery.

In recent years, developed countries have witnessed a dramatic increase in the number of cosmetic procedures being performed annually (e.g., American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery, 2008), particularly among young people (e.g., Zuckerman & Abraham, 2008). This increase is partly motivated by more positive attitudes toward cosmetic surgery as a means of appearanceenhancement (Sarwer et al., 2005; Sarwer & Magee, 2006). More generally, Sarwer and colleagues (Sarwer, Crerand, & Gibbons, 2007; Sarwer & Magee, 2006; Sarwer, Magee, & Crerand, 2003) have related the increasing popularity of cosmetic surgery to higher disposable incomes among patients, the lower cost of procedures, and increased media coverage of cosmetic procedures.

Given these developments, it is no surprise that psychologists have focused their attention on correlates of interest in cosmetic surgery. For example, recent work has reported that women are much more willing than men to undergo cosmetic procedures (e.g., Brown, Furnham, Glanville, & Swami, 2007; Swami, Arteche, et al., 2008), which is consistent with the actual female-to-male ratio of cosmetic patients standing at 9:1 (American Society for Plastic Surgeons, 2008). Other work has shown significant associations between willingness to undergo cosmetic surgery and respondent age (Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005), self-assessed

attractiveness (Brown et al., 2007; Swami, Chamorro-Premuzic, Bridges, & Furnham, 2009), media exposure (Sperry, Thompson, Sarwer, & Cash, 2009), appearance-based rejection sensitivity (Park, Calogero, Harwin, & DiRaddo, 2009), and negative body image (Cash, Goldenberg-Bivens, & Grasso, 2005; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005; von Soest, Kvalem, Skolleborg, & Roald, 2006).

Although a number of different scales exist to measure willingness to undergo cosmetic surgery (e.g., Brown et al., 2007; von Soest et al., 2006), perhaps the most reliable is Henderson-King and Henderson-King's (2005) Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale (ACSS). The ACSS measures three aspects of attitudinal dispositions toward cosmetic surgery, namely attitudes related to the selforiented benefits of having cosmetic surgery (Interpersonal), social motivations that influence the decision to have cosmetic surgery (Social), and the self-reported likelihood of respondents having cosmetic surgery (Consider). The extant literature has documented significant associations between these ACSS subscales and body image disturbance (Cash et al., 2005; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005), exposure to reality cosmetic surgery television programmes (Sperry et al., 2009), the Big Five personality factors (Swami, Chamorro-Premuzic, et al., 2009), celebrity worship (Swami, Taylor, & Carvalho, 2009), materialist values and paternal attitudes (Henderson-King & Brooks, 2009).

The present study sought to extend this body of research by examining the association between the Consider subscale of the ACSS (which directly measures future interest and likelihood in having cosmetic surgery, rather than attitudinal dispositions about cosmetic surgery) and body appreciation, media influence, and

respondentweight status and age. Based on previouswork (e.g.,Cash et al., 2005; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005; Sperry et al., 2009; Swami, Chamorro-Premuzic, et al., 2009), itwas predicted that participants with less body appreciation, higher internalisation of media influence, a higher body mass index (BMI), and older age would report greater consideration of cosmetic surgery.

The participants of this study were 322 female university students enrolled in a number of courses at a university in Greater London (age M = 24.72, SD = 5.90; BMI M = 21.67, SD = 3.48). The majority of participants were of European Caucasian descent (63.7%), while the remainder were of Asian descent (13.7%), African Caribbean descent (13.7%), or other ancestry (9.0%). Most participants self-reported as being atheists (40.1%), while others were Christians (23.9%), unsure of their religious beliefs (12.4%), Muslims (8.7%), or of some other religious background (14.9%).
Consideration of cosmetic surgery (Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005)

Consideration of cosmetic surgery was measured using the Consider subscale of the ACSS, which contains five items assessing the likelihood that a respondent would consider having cosmetic surgery. All items were rated on a 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly disagree,7= Strongly agree) and an overall score was computed by taking the mean of the five items. Previous work has shown that this subscale has high internal consistency, good test– retest reliability, and good convergent and discriminant validity (Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005). In the present study, Cronbach's alpha for this subscale was .92.
Sociocultural Attitudes Towards Appearance Questionnaire-3 (SATAQ-3; Thompson, van den Berg, Roehrig, Guarda, & Heinberg, 2004)

Media influences were measured using the SATAQ-3, a 30-item scale measuring the multi-dimensional impact of sociocultural influences on body image. The scale consists of four factors measuring the degree to which various media are considered an important source of information about being attractive (Information), feeling pressured by various media to strive for cultural ideals of beauty (Pressure), endorsement and acceptance of media messages touting unrealistic ideals for female beauty and the striving towards these ideals (Internalisation-General), and endorsement and acceptance of an athletic and toned body ideal (Internalisation-Athlete). The four factors are internally reliable, with Cronbach's alpha coefficients generally exceeding .80 (e.g.,

Thompson et al., 2004). Items were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = Definitely disagree, 5= Definitely agree), and subscale scores were computed by taking the mean of items associated with each factor. In the present study, Cronbach's alpha coefficients were as follows: Information, .87; Pressure, .83; Internalisation-General, .91, and; Internalisation-Athlete, .93.
Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005)

The BAS, which measures aspects of positive body image, is a 13-item scale that has been shown to have a unidimensional structure when completed by Western women (Avalos et al., 2005; Swami, Stieger, Haubner, & Voracek, 2008), with good test–retest reliability (Avalos et al., 2005) and good construct and discriminant validity (Avalos et al., 2005; Swami, Stieger, et al., 2008). All items were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = Never, 5= Always) and responses on all 13 items were averaged to obtain an overall BAS score (higher scores reflected greater body appreciation). Cronbach's alpha for this scale was .90.
All participants provided their demographic details consisting of age, ethnicity, religion, height, and weight. The latter two items were used to calculate participants' BMI, as kg/m2 .

Once ethical approval for this study was obtained from the relevant university ethics committee, participants were recruited opportunistically from various campus locations (e.g., libraries, cafeterias). The nature of the experiment was explained and, once participants provided informed consent, they were given a paperand-pencil questionnaire to complete individually and anonymously. Participants were given a description of the study and completed a paper-and-pencil questionnaire after providing informed consent. They were verbally debriefed once they returned their completed questionnaires. All participants took part on a voluntary basis and were not remunerated for their time.

Descriptive statistics (Ms and SDs) for all variables and interitem correlations are reported in Table 1. As can be seen from Table 1, consideration of cosmetic surgery was significantly and positively correlated with three of the SATAQ-3 subscales (Information, Pressures, and Internalisation-General) and significantly and negatively correlated with body appreciation, BMI, and age. Even so, it should be noted that these significant correlations were likely inflated by the large sample size. To examine predictors of consideration of cosmetic surgery, the remaining variables were entered as predictors in a multiple linear regression.
Table 1 Descriptive statistics and inter-item correlations between consideration of cosmetic surgery, media influence, body appreciation, weight status, and age.
Note: SATAQ-3 = Sociocultural Attitudes Towards Appearance Questionnaire (3rd revision), BAS = Body Appreciation Scale, BMI = Body Mass Index.

The results of the current study showed that body appreciation. media influence, and respondent weight status were significant predictors of consideration of cosmetic surgery among female undergraduates, explaining 47.1% of the variance. Of the variables entered into the regression model, the strongest predictor was body appreciation, which is consistent with previous work showing that negative body image is associated with more positive attitudes toward cosmetic surgery (e.g., Cash et al., 2005; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005; von Soest et al., 2006). That is, individuals who have negative self-perceptions of their attractiveness or are dissatisfied with their appearance may view cosmetic surgery as a means of repairing damaged selfconcepts (Sarwer et al., 2005; Sarwer & Magee, 2006). More generally, the current results suggest that it is important to consider not just objective measures of appearance such as BMI, but also subjective perceptions of one's body.

The current study also extends previous work in showing that three of the SATAQ-3 subscales were significant predictors of consideration of cosmetic surgery. In general, these results suggest that there is a greater desire to have cosmetic surgery among women who perceive media messages as informative about physical appearance and who internalise those messages. These results are consistent with previous commentary that increased media coverage of cosmetic procedures is, in part at least, driving the greater popularity of such procedures (e.g., Sarwer et al., 2003). This is further corroborated by research showing that viewership of reality cosmetic surgery television shows was related to acceptance of cosmetic surgery (Sperry et al., 2009), although in that study acceptance of cosmetic surgery was measured using total scores from the ACSS.

Two further results are worthy of consideration in the present study. First, although participant BMI was a significant predictor of consideration of cosmetic surgery, it was not in the predicted direction (i.e., more slender participants reported greater consideration of cosmetic surgery). Second, respondent age was significantly and negative correlated with consideration of cosmetic surgery, but did not emerge as a significant predictor. Both of these results may be a reflection of the select sample of participants in the present study (i.e., undergraduate women), for whom the range of BMIs and age was relatively constricted. As such, these results may not be generalisable to other sample of women and it would be beneficial to replicate the current work using representative samples from the community.

A further limitation of the present study was the limited number of variables included in the design, which possibly obscured other psychological variables that may mediate the relationships between tested constructs. It is conceivable, for example, that the predictive power of body appreciation, media influence, and participant demographics would be attenuated should other variables have been included in the present study. Future work could, therefore, extend the current research by
including other relevant variables, such as self-esteem, the Big Five personality factors, self-objectification, and sexist attitudes.

In conclusion, the results of the present study showed that negative body appreciation, media influence, and weight status predicted consideration of cosmetic surgery. These results may have important implications for practitioners and patients who view cosmetic surgery as a means of appearance-enhancement. For instance, given mixed results of the association between cosmetic surgery and improved body image (for a review, see Cook, Rosser, & Salmon, 2006), psychological screening for potential patients may not go amiss (e.g., Zuckerman & Abraham, 2008). More generally, promoting more positive body appreciation and inoculating women against media messages about beauty ideals may assist potential patients to make more educated decisions about cosmetic surgery and its effects on self-perceptions.
